item.title: Key role of services trade highlighted
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
Key role of services trade highlighted Services: Increasing demand seen for high-quality imports China will further open its services sector, ease market access and expand imports of high-quality services as it seeks to create new growth drivers for trade in services and share the opportunities of its vast market with the world, government officials said on Wednesday. Speaking at the opening ceremony of the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services in Beijing on Wednesday, Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang said China will further refine the negative list for cross-border trade in services, widen market access in the services sector and foster a more favorable business environment. Ding, who is also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said the nation will accelerate the development of new business forms and models such as digital services trade, develop knowledge-intensive services and expand exports of producer services. The 2026 CIFTIS, which runs through Sunday, has drawn participants from 90 countries, regions and international organizations. More than 1,800 companies, including Honeywell, McDonald's and Schneider Electric, are exhibiting on-site. More than 100 new products and services will make their debut at the fair, covering fields such as information and communications, financial technology, and digital and intelligent healthcare. Against a backdrop of growing uncertainty in the global trading system, officials from international organizations and foreign governments said during the fair's opening ceremony that services are set to play an increasingly important role in global trade and supply chains. Johanna Hill, deputy director-general of the World Trade Organization, said services are becoming an increasingly important part of global supply chains, supporting not only production but also design, management, logistics and distribution. She said China can contribute to global services trade by demonstrating the benefits of more competitive services markets and sharing its experience with developing economies. Highlighting the opportunities for developing economies, Constantino Chiwenga, the Zimbabwean vice-president, said automation and digital innovation are reshaping the global economy and creating new opportunities for trade in services. Zimbabwe is seeking deeper services cooperation with China through investment, technology transfer and skills development in areas including healthcare, financial services, transportation and professional services, he said. Alexander Poulev, Bulgaria's deputy prime minister and minister of economy, investments and industry, said trade in services is a key pillar of Bulgaria-China economic ties, with the country seeking stronger long-term partnerships with Chinese businesses. "Stronger investment cooperation could create new supply chains and add greater value to bilateral trade," Poulev said. Policy push Advancing the high-quality development of services trade is a key task outlined in China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), which calls for intensified efforts to optimize negative list management of services trade, ease cross-border restrictions, encourage services exports and foster knowledge-intensive services trade. Digitalization and emerging technologies are expected to play an increasingly important role in reshaping the services sector and expanding cross-border trade. Yin Li, a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and secretary of the CPC Beijing Municipal Committee, said Beijing stands ready to work with global partners to facilitate trade flows, expand services trade and share the opportunities of China's vast market. China's trade in services totaled nearly 4.45 trillion yuan ($663 billion) in the first seven months of this year, up 8.3 percent year-on-year, data from the Ministry of Commerce showed. The expansion of services trade is also translating into new opportunities for companies across a range of sectors. James Evans, general manager of Cathay Cargo, a business unit of the Hong Kong-based Cathay Group, said the company sees the Chinese mainland's continued industrial upgrading, expanding global trade links and increasingly diversified import demand as important drivers. "On the import side, temperature-controlled cargo is performing particularly well," Evans said. "We are seeing increasing demand for the transportation of fresh produce and pharmaceuticals into the Chinese mainland, reflecting rising consumer demand for high-quality imported goods and the growing importance of reliable cold-chain logistics." State-owned Shenyang Northern Aircraft Maintenance and Engineering Co in Shenyang, Liaoning province, handled 46 million yuan worth of imports and exports between January and August under the bonded maintenance model, a customs arrangement that allows companies to import faulty or damaged foreign-made products without paying import duties, provided they are repaired and then reexported. Five auxiliary power units, or APUs, were repaired and delivered during the period, according to Shenyang Customs. Wang Lulu, the company's president, said the company will seek more orders from foreign airlines and expand high-end producer services, including APU testing, maintenance and overhaul, particularly in Central and Southeast Asia.

item.title: China's fishing ban experience commended
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
China's fishing ban experience commended Experts highlight gains in biodiversity and measures to safeguard livelihoods Experts at a United Nations event have highlighted China's experience in implementing a 10-year fishing ban in key waters of the Yangtze River basin, citing gains in aquatic biodiversity and support for former fishers. From 2021 to 2025, 351 native fish species were recorded across the basin, 43 more than before the ban, according to data released by China's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs at the 37th Session of the Committee on Fisheries of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. The population of the Yangtze finless porpoise, a flagship species of the basin, also rose from a historical low of 1,012 in 2017 to 1,426 in 2025. Zhuang Ping, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Fishery Sciences, said effective resettlement and livelihood support for former fishers was essential to sustaining the ban. Over the past five years, the Chinese government has registered 231,000 former fishers and provided assistance based on their circumstances, Zhuang said. By the end of June, nearly all of the 139,000 who were able and willing to work had found employment, while 220,000 eligible former fishers had full pension coverage. Another 12,000 former fishers facing difficulties received minimum living allowances or temporary assistance. China's experience highlights a broader challenge in conservation: restrictions aimed at protecting aquatic resources are hard to sustain unless affected communities have viable livelihoods. Zhuang said law enforcement and supervision, along with the systematic protection and restoration of aquatic ecosystems, were equally important. Over the past five years, China has strengthened joint law enforcement and routine supervision, enhanced enforcement capacity and promoted the use of high-tech tools such as radar and drones. He summarized China's experience in five principles: putting people first, prioritizing ecology, pursuing law-based governance, balancing different interests and building broad consensus. Chen Jie, a researcher at the agriculture ministry, said the ban has not ended the Yangtze's thousands of years of fishing culture. Instead, it has created an opportunity for the culture to evolve, shifting its preservation from fishing production to heritage protection, education and cultural activities. "We have established fishing culture museums at different levels and dedicated exhibition venues, using virtual reality and reconstructed real-life scenes to tell stories of the Yangtze's ecology to the public, particularly young people," Chen said. "We have also promoted traditional folk activities, which have helped boost the rural nighttime tourism economy." Localities have also used geographical-indication aquatic products, intangible cultural heritage-inspired creative products, science education and popular science initiatives to build distinctive and influential Yangtze fishing-culture brands, bringing elements of the culture closer to consumers through market-oriented products, she said. More importantly, China has established the principle that "those who protect should benefit", she added. Former fishers have received compensation for giving up fishing rights and scrapping boats and nets, subsidies for pension contributions, and transitional living allowances. They have also found stable employment through jobs such as ecological patrols and positions created through industrial transformation. Well-being of fishers Muhammad Farhan Khan, a delegate from Pakistan, said he was moved by China's presentation on the well-being of fishers. "Pakistan has always been a flag-bearer for protecting small-scale fisheries and fishermen," he said. "We recognize the measures and actions taken by the Chinese government, and we would like to see similar practices in Pakistan and explore possible cooperation with China." Henning Winker, a stock assessment frameworks specialist with the Secretariat of the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean in Italy, said he was "fascinated by the scale and strength" of the Yangtze fishing ban. "From the presentation and related scientific literature, I understand that China has achieved very impressive results in restoring aquatic biodiversity and protecting the ecological environment," he said. "Achieving this requires very strong governance — not only to enforce fishing ban measures, but also to compensate fishers; combat illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing; and ensure effective ecological restoration and monitoring."

item.title: Digital tech helps drive travel industry growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
Digital tech helps drive travel industry growth 'China Bound·Beijing' smart English cultural tourism platform launched While digital technologies are reshaping the tourism industry and making travel more efficient and accessible, they can also foster human connections and cooperation, and safeguard communities and culture to drive tourism growth, participants at a cultural and tourism event said on Wednesday. They made the remarks during the opening ceremony of the World Conference on Tourism Cooperation and Development 2026 in Beijing's Shougang Park. Hosted by the World Tourism Cities Federation, or WTCF, and co-organized by the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism, the conference attracted representatives of the WTCF's member cities, heads of international organizations, cross-border travel traders, diplomatic envoys to China and experts from more than 50 countries and regions. Themed "Smart Tourism, Shared Prosperity", the conference runs through Friday and is being held amid the ongoing 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services. "Our responsibility is not to choose between residents and visitors, but to build a model in which both can thrive. Smart tourism gives us practical tools to achieve this balance. For example, digital platforms can improve accessibility, multilingual information and journey planning," said Olaf McKay, mayor of Valletta, the capital of Malta. He added that China's visa-free policy is making the country more accessible for Maltese citizens, especially young people and students, enabling them to experience China's traditions and culture firsthand. Ben Montgomery, vice-chairwoman of the Pacific Asia Travel Association, a not-for-profit membership association headquartered in Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, agreed. "Artificial intelligence, data analytics and digital platforms are reshaping how people discover, book and experience destinations worldwide. As we embrace these tools, we must remember a fundamental truth: Tourism is ultimately about people," she said. She added that the true value of the tourism industry lies in human connection — by linking visitors with local communities, bridging cultures and fostering shared understanding across borders. "Beijing is a city where centuries of rich history seamlessly meet modern innovation. … Today is about turning ideas into practical collaborations through partnerships, matchmaking and open exchanges," Montgomery said. Dai Bin, director of the China Tourism Academy, noted that tourism allows international visitors to get close to authentic daily life in China and try out Chinese services. He said that Beijing has rolled out a number of AI-backed, visitor-friendly initiatives, such as cross-regional tax refunds, providing a referable model for AI-driven cultural and tourism applications. Joseph Daniel Lema, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, the United States, unveiled the World Tourism Cities Development Report (2025-26) by the WTCF at the event. The report examines the opportunities and challenges in safety governance, technology adoption, industrial integration, cultural heritage, brand building and regional coordination, and offers forward-looking and actionable policy recommendations. The top 10 cities in the World Tourism Cities Development Comprehensive Ranking are New York, Tokyo, Paris, London, Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Milan, Istanbul and Dubai. "Beijing has moved up its ranking, reflecting the strength of cultural resources, smart governance and safety assurance," Lema said. One-stop gateway At the conference, China Daily and the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism jointly launched the "China Bound·Beijing" English cultural tourism platform, offering international visitors a new one-stop gateway to explore Beijing. The smart platform includes an English-language website (chinabound.cn/beijing), as well as dedicated pages on the Alipay and WeChat mini-programs of China Bound. It provides services ranging from itinerary planning to AI-powered assistance, enabling overseas travelers to experience the unique beauty of Beijing. "We aim to tell Beijing's cultural-tourism stories in a language overseas audiences understand, and translate the city's resource advantages into inbound tourism appeal. We promote immersive experiences such as intangible cultural heritage to enable inbound visitors to stay longer for in-depth travel," said Zheng Fang, deputy director of the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism. xulin@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Former superstar hurdler Liu donates entire salary to charity
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
Former superstar hurdler Liu donates entire salary to charity Olympic champion Liu Xiang said on Thursday that he completed a buyout with Shanghai sports authorities on Sept 1, receiving 494,000 yuan, and would have no further association with the sports bureau. “On Sept 1, I had already completed the buyout and received 494,000 yuan in buyout compensation,” Liu said in a post on his personal social media account. “From now on, I will have no further association with the sports bureau.” The 43-year-old former hurdler also said that he had received a total of 982,935 yuan in salary and subsidies from April 7, 2015, when he retired, until the completion of the buyout. Liu said he donated the entire amount to the China Charity Federation on Sept 2 for disaster relief following mudslides in the Xizang autonomous region. Liu's latest post came after a public dispute over his post-retirement career arrangement triggered widespread discussion on Chinese social media. On Aug 26, Liu posted a photo commemorating his victory at the 2004 Athens Olympics and said the sports authorities had asked him to choose between becoming a coach and accepting a buyout. The Shanghai Sports Bureau said afterward that Liu was an outstanding athlete who had made significant contributions to Shanghai's sports development. It said the Shanghai Competitive Sports Training Management Center had communicated with Liu and would handle his post-retirement arrangement in accordance with relevant national and municipal regulations, mainly through organizational placement or self-employment. In his latest post, Liu also addressed what he described as the issue of being “on the payroll but not at his post”, saying he had not received any formal position or post since his retirement. “I have not received any official post or position since I retired,” Liu said. “I respect the rules and accept that there may have been oversights, but rules should never be an excuse.” He questioned why the issue had taken 11 years to address, saying that the choice between becoming a coach and accepting a buyout had come too late to be regarded as a genuine career choice. Liu said he hoped his case would encourage greater attention to the career transition of retired athletes and called for more flexible and diverse arrangements. “Putting the issue of resettlement in the public eye is not about using public opinion to seek a third option,” he said. “I hope organizations will seriously consider the future of every retired athlete and treat them well.” Liu won the men's 110-meter hurdles at the 2004 Athens Olympics with a time of 12.91 seconds, becoming the first Asian athlete to win an Olympic gold medal in a men's track event. He went on to win the world title in 2007 and set a world record of 12.88 seconds in 2006.

item.title: Hotel robots surprise visitors, streamline operations
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
When Ricky Colomer Goenaga, 32, a designer from Spain, looked around and noticed a delivery robot following him, he wasn't quite sure how to react. New to Shanghai and living at a hotel, he stepped into an elevator — and a white, waist-high box on wheels followed him in. The robot, in Goenaga's words, was rather assertive. It nudged him out of the middle of the elevator, nearly ran over his toes and rattled off something in Chinese he didn't understand. Then it pressed the button for its desired floor and rolled out as soon as the elevator doors opened. "I was like, 'what happened here?'" Goenaga recalled. He said that he wasn't quite sure what the machine even was — bigger and bulkier than, yet nothing like, the robotic vacuums he'd seen. One and a half years on, the sight of a robot gliding through hotel lobbies and corridors no longer fazes him. In March, on a business trip to Beijing, he keyed his room number into the order system and waited. Soon, the robot arrived at his door carrying his packed salad. This time, Goenaga was all grins. He posed for a photograph with the machine and posted it on social media, joking that after being "bullied" by the robot in Shanghai, the two had finally made peace. For many foreign visitors, the robot is among the first surprises they encounter in China. Social media are full of posts about their "meetings" with the machines in their hotels, with comments such as "I'm sharing the elevator with robots!" or "China is on another level of efficiency". In China, however, such robots are no longer a novelty. According to a report released in August by IIM, a Beijing-based industry research organization, the penetration rate of hotel service robots in China exceeded 30 percent in 2025 and is expected to surpass 50 percent by 2030. For hotels, the appeal is simple: Robots can handle repetitive tasks around the clock. "I think they are very useful. They save us plenty of time and improve the efficiency," said Wang Xinyu, a lobby manager at a budget hotel in Beijing. Open since January, the hotel operates three robots across six floors and 372 rooms. Wang said that more than half the guests order takeaway during mealtimes — and that last stretch, from front desk to door, is where the robots step in. When an order lands, the front desk tucks the food into the robot's compartment and punches in the room number. From there, the robot owns it — it hails the elevator, rolls to the door and pings the guest to come grab it. Between rushes, the machines remain parked in corners, charging their batteries. Autoxing Technology Co, the company that makes the robots, was founded in 2020 with ambitions to develop autonomous-driving technology for cars. But the bet proved expensive, prompting the company to narrow its focus. Two years later, it launched its hotel robots. The technology behind them is largely the same, enabling machines to move from one place to another without bumping into any obstacles. "The rapid development of autonomous-driving in China has, to some extent, boosted other robotic applications," said Yang Tianyun, a marketing manager at Autoxing. About 60 percent of Autoxing's business now comes from exports, although differences in regulations across countries can slow deployment. This helps explain why the robots can surprise foreign visitors like Goenaga. "We had never seen anything like that anywhere else in the world," Goenaga said. "I think a lot of people are not aware of how advanced the technology is here." As a designer, Goenaga also likes the robots' cute look. They do not need to look human, he said, adding that a friendly, approachable design is more fitting for hotels, where they interact with families and children.

item.title: Digging deep, working together
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
Digging deep, working together Greater cooperation called for as global mining heads toward greener, smarter future Editor's note: The 2026 China Mining Conference and Exhibition opens in Tianjin on Thursday and will run until Saturday. Over the three days, 28 forums will be held and the exhibition area will cover 65,000 square meters. On this page, we've invited Liu Guohong, Party secretary of the Ministry of Natural Resources of China, which hosts the event, and six senior officials of foreign countries to share their thoughts on the prospects of the industry. Currently, a new round of scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation is evolving at an accelerating pace. The energy transition and the rise of emerging industries have presented significant opportunities for the development of the global mining industry. Meanwhile, intertwined factors such as geopolitical conflicts, trade barriers and climate change have also brought uncertainties to global mining development. How to balance development and security, exploitation and protection, as well as the present and the long term has become a common issue for the international community. Under the theme of "win-win cooperation, green and intelligent development", the 2026 China Mining Conference and Exhibition aims to conform to the prevailing trends and respond to the expectations of all parties. Cooperation is the only way to achieve prosperity in the mining industry. As a Chinese proverb goes: "It is difficult to lift heavy objects alone, but easy to move forward when walking together." Mineral resources are unevenly distributed across the world, making it inevitable for industrial and supply chains to be interconnected across borders and mutually dependent. History has repeatedly proven that isolation and fragmentation lead nowhere, while openness and cooperation are the right path forward. True resource security should be built upon diversified supply and mutual trust. China has always adhered to multilateralism, promoted the building of an open world economy, continuously relaxed market access for foreign investment, and optimized the business environment. We have actively participated in global mining governance and worked to maintain the stability of the global mining market. Looking ahead, we are willing to deepen cooperation with all parties in areas such as exploration and mining, technology and equipment, standards and regulations, and talent training. We will also facilitate infrastructure development, boost economic growth and create more jobs, ensuring that the dividends of cooperation benefit all parties fairly, and jointly safeguarding the security and stability of global industrial and supply chains. Green is the defining feature of the mining industry's transformation. Humanity and nature form a community of life. China actively practices the concept that "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets". We are committed to a path that coordinates mineral development with ecological protection, comprehensively advancing green exploration, improving green mining standards, promoting resource-saving and intensive technologies, implementing ecological restoration of mining areas, and vigorously constructing green mines. Furthermore, the green transformation of the mining industry has been enshrined in the newly revised Mineral Resources Law. We are ready to share our experience in green mine construction with countries around the world, deepen cooperation in green mine standards, technologies and management, jointly promote the low-carbon transition of the global mining sector, better protect the ecological environment, actively respond to and mitigate global climate change, and jointly safeguard the beautiful homeland of humanity. Intelligent technology is a powerful engine driving the upgrading of the mining industry. As an old Chinese saying goes: "The wise observe the trends, but those who harness them win." As mineral exploration and development extend deeper into the Earth, technological progress has become the driving force for high-quality development in the mining industry. It is imperative to accelerate the integration of new technologies such as artificial intelligence, big data, cloud computing, the internet of things and 5G to reshape industrial forms and production methods. China is actively promoting the construction of intelligent mines, with unmanned mining trucks, remote mining control systems and digital twin management platforms already being widely applied in mineral development. We look forward to deepening technological exchanges, recognizing mutual standards and collaborative innovation with countries around the world, ensuring that the fruits of digital intelligence benefit all nations equitably and jointly enhancing the modernization level of the global mining industry. Since its inception in 1999, the China Mining Conference and Exhibition has been successfully held for 27 sessions. Integrating themed forums, exhibitions, project promotions, policy releases and signing ceremonies, the conference sees extensive participation from government departments, mining enterprises, financial institutions, research institutes and international organizations from various countries. It has become a high-end platform for exchanges and cooperation in the international mining community and an important window for observing global mining development trends. This year's conference merges the international mining ministers' forum with the opening ceremony. The number of participating countries, ministerial-level guests from abroad, and registered enterprises and representatives have all reached record highs, demonstrating the global mining sector's strong desire for multilateral dialogue and practical cooperation. China is willing to work with all countries to make good use of this platform, facilitate the reform and improvement of the global mining governance system, and jointly promote the steady and long-term development of the global mining industry. A just cause enjoys abundant support; the world is a family. The world is striving to build a sustainable and bright future, and a prosperous mining industry will provide strong support for achieving this goal. In the face of both opportunities and challenges, only through open cooperation can we transform resource endowments into common wealth; only through green development can we achieve a win-win situation between industrial prosperity and ecological protection; and only through technological innovation can we expand new horizons for mining development. China is ready to join hands with all countries, gathering strength through cooperation, safeguarding the future with green initiatives, and driving development with intelligent technologies. Together, we will promote the building of a more equitable, open, inclusive, shared, stable and sustainable new global mining governance landscape, and jointly create a bright future for global mining development. I wish this conference a complete success. I wish all distinguished guests smooth work and good health. The author is the Party secretary of the Ministry of Natural Resources. The views don't necessarily represent those of China Daily.

item.title: Tiangong class inspires Hong Kong, Macao students
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
Tiangong class inspires Hong Kong, Macao students A live-broadcast class given on Wednesday by the in-orbit Shenzhou XXIII crew, including Lai Ka-ying, the first astronaut from Hong Kong to travel into space, ignited a passion among students in the Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions for exploring space and inspired them to contribute to national aerospace exploration in the future. The 90-minute class, a special session for Hong Kong and Macao students under the Tiangong Class series, was beamed from China's Tiangong space station to the students starting at 9:50 am local time. Three astronauts — Lai, the mission's payload specialist, commander Zhu Yangzhu and pilot Zhang Zhiyuan — shared their knowledge and experiences with the students. They demonstrated several phenomena in a zero-gravity environment, including using a towel-covered table tennis paddle to strike a water droplet, which bounced off the towel just like a ping-pong ball. The astronauts also explained the space station's living facilities and food supplies. Education authorities in Hong Kong and Macao encouraged all local primary and secondary schools to arrange for students and teachers to watch the broadcast from their own classrooms. Students at Lai's alma mater, Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College, watched the class in a specially designated space, and were joined by 60 students and educators from 15 Macao schools. Addressing the audience gathered at the school, Hong Kong SAR Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the class gave Hong Kong and Macao students the opportunity to interact with astronauts aboard Tiangong and to appreciate the nation's aerospace achievements and ambitions. Lee said that Lai, who was born and raised in Hong Kong, has shown that the space dream is never out of reach. Hong Kong people can also contribute to the nation's aerospace endeavors, he said, adding that scientists in Hong Kong have provided equipment and technical support for the country's lunar, Martian and other space exploration missions. Eight students — six from Hong Kong and two from Macao — asked the three astronauts questions during the real-time dialogue session. A Hong Kong primary school student asked what kind of preparations astronauts make before a spacewalk and what psychological and physiological experiences they undergo during extravehicular activities. Zhu said the crewmembers rehearse with equipment, conduct drills, examine spacesuits and monitor their physical condition before a spacewalk. Although spacewalks are physically grueling, he added, looking out into space gives the astronauts a real sense of what exploring the universe is all about. Doris Cheong Weng-man, from Macao's Sacred Heart Canossian College, English Section, asked what the astronauts considered to be the most profound challenges they faced during training. Lai said the most memorable ones included desert survival training, sleep deprivation training and a six-day cave training session. "The training posed significant physical and psychological challenges, and made me realize the importance of discipline and teamwork," she added. At Pui Kiu Middle School in Hong Kong, more than 100 students gathered to watch the class. In 2003, China's first in-orbit astronaut, Yang Liwei, planted an oak tree at the school during his visit to the Hong Kong SAR. Kwan See-heng, a 10th-grade student, said that this was the first time he had witnessed a class presented via a live question-and-answer session. "As a student of science, I hope to get involved in scientific research and development, and to contribute to space technologies if given the chance," Kwan said. William Xu, Li Xiang and Flora Ni contributed to this story. atlasshao@chinadailyhk.com

item.title: Preserving the soul and waterways that keep history alive
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
Editor's note: A number of Chinese cities have maintained their cultural memory in the form of historical neighborhoods that have only added to their multilayered charm and vigor with the passage of time. China Daily is taking readers on a journey to some of these timeless areas, where efforts on the preservation and vitalization of heritage are setting examples. In this installment, we wander about Yunnan province's Old Town of Lijiang, which remains as a thriving community where customs are woven into the everyday. Mu Li usually wakes to the sound of running water. "When I was a child, we fetched drinking water from the river before 6 am. After that, the river was for washing vegetables and clothes," recalls Mu, who was born and raised in the Old Town of Lijiang, Southwest China's Yunnan province. "The elders always told us: Never throw anything into the river, or your mouth will rot." For generations, such unwritten rules had governed daily life in the Old Town, where waterways have long been both a lifeline and a guardian. Mu still prefers to describe herself simply as "a child who grew up in the Old Town". For more than two decades, she has worked in a series of local government roles dedicated to the ancient town's management and preservation. "I've never really left," she says. Founded during the late Song (960-1279) and early Yuan (1271-1368) dynasties, the Old Town of Lijiang has stood for about 800 years. According to Mu, people of the Naxi ethnic group first established settlements in Baisha, an ancient town north of Lijiang, before gradually moving south to Dayan — the historical name for the area that later became today's Lijiang Old Town. Drawn by a basin sheltered by surrounding mountains, they built their homes around the waterways. "The mountains block the wind and keep the valley warm," Mu says. They diverted a single stream through the settlement. Over time, it branched into three waterways, around which houses, lanes and markets gradually took shape, following the natural contours of the land. "Few settlements of this scale have preserved such an integrated water system," Mu says. More than 350 stone and wood bridges link homes, courtyards and winding alleys. Water has never been merely ornamental. It supplied drinking water, sustained daily life and agriculture, and helped regulate floods. Every week, residents near the town's Sifang Square still open the wooden sluice gates to release water from the Yuhe (Jade) River, allowing it to cascade down the gently sloping square and wash the stone streets clean. "The covers used to be open," Mu says with a laugh. "But tourists kept falling in, so we had to close them." Even the paving stones tell a story. The streets are paved with locally quarried five-colored stone from Yulong (Jade Dragon) Snow Mountain, traditionally known as wuhuashi. Today, many locals call it "Unity Stone". "People of the Han, Bai, Yi, Tibetan, and Naxi ethnic groups have lived and traded here for centuries. The new name reflects that shared history," Mu says. Refusing to sell A few steps away from the bustling streets stands Hengyugong, a traditional courtyard completed in 1875. It is a classic Naxi residence, featuring a four-sided courtyard. Covering more than 600 square meters, the compound comprises four wings arranged around a central quadrangle. The courtyard still holds Qing Dynasty (1644-1911) gilded carvings on its doors and windows. Li Junxing, affectionately known as "Uncle Six", is its fourth-generation keeper. "I've been running this museum for 16 years," he says. "It's a living museum because we still live here." Visitors tour the front courtyard while his family continues everyday life in the rear residence, separated only by a single wooden door. When a devastating earthquake struck Lijiang in 1996, Hengyugong emerged almost unscathed. "Look at the walls," Li says, pointing to the weathered masonry. "There isn't a crack. The whole courtyard stays level." The Li family traces its roots in Lijiang back about 400 years, when their ancestors arrived from Nanjing, Jiangsu province, to serve the Mu family. During the Qing Dynasty, the family shifted from scholarship to commerce, establishing the Hengyugong trading house in 1868. The present courtyard followed seven years later. Every morning, Li wipes down the wooden doors and sweeps the courtyard before welcoming visitors. "A house needs people. Only when people live in it does it stay alive," he says. In the center of the courtyard lies a pebble mosaic resembling an ancient copper coin. At its center sits a raised stone. "This is our family's stumbling stone. Every time someone trips over it, they're reminded not to stumble over money." Every object, Li emphasizes, has been passed down within the family. He usually opens an old account book dating to the late Qing Dynasty when greeting guests. "It tells us what our great-grandfather was doing. He traded silk with the Jiangnan region (the southern regions of the lower reaches of the Yangtze River)," he says. Carved wooden panels, porcelain and an old pair of eyeglasses fashioned from bamboo sit nearby. Buyers have been knocking on the family's door for decades. Each time, Li turned down the offer. "An ancestral home cannot be sold," he says.
